title: How and Why We Split One Managed ELT Box into Three Components We Control
body_markdown:
*Written By:*[Amin Ziaei](https://www.linkedin.com/in/aminziaei/)


We recently launched a project that I led to build our own self-hosted Extract, Load, Transform (ELT) solution for our data pipelines. The reasons were threefold: to gain more control over the scalability and availability of our data pipelines; to give us more technical flexibility in the tools we can use for those pipelines; and to find a cheaper alternative to the tool we had been using (a SaaS solution).


What follows is an overview of this project and a guide for others to do the same, including how to set up the stack, what each tool is responsible for and how to make the full ELT solution production-ready for critical data pipelines within your system. The stack consists of just three tools, Airbyte, DBT and Airflow, each of which performs a distinct role, as follows:


### Baseline: A Self-Hosted Three-Tool ELT Stack for Critical Data Components


Here’s what each component performs as part of a full ELT solution:


- Airbyte: Extract and load data from a source database to a destination database
- DBT: Transformation of the data loaded into the destination database
- Airflow: Orchestration between DBT and Airbyte, such as scheduling and monitoring tools


Here’s a bit more on how each tool functions within the full ELT solution and why it was the best option for our purposes.


#### Airbyte


Airbyte is a self-hosted cluster that spins up a number of pods within your Kubernetes cluster, with a dedicated task to successfully extract data from a source database and transfer it to a destination database.


We chose this tool because its concepts are simple to grasp, with no code or complex logic needed to move data between databases, thanks to its easy-to-use UI and admin APIs. That said, Airbyte is a heavy tool; it requires many components to set up, which makes it difficult to run on a local machine. Airbyte also has some pitfalls we learned over time while using it in production, which I’ll elaborate on in the Production Readiness section below.


Airbyte includes the following components:


- **Sources:** Airbyte has a massive selection of options. Each database source needs to be installed on your Airbyte instance through its admin UI. When defining a source, you are presented with configuration options specific to the database you’re connecting to.
- **Destinations** : Airbyte also offers a comprehensive list of database types to choose from, with configuration options specific to each type.
- **Connections:** Airbyte connects a source to a destination and also holds configurations for the schema, the type of data sync that works best with your data (incremental, full refresh, etc.), the source database and other general configurations, such as which schema to push to if not defined in the destination configuration.


The type of data sync options you are presented with depends on:


- **Source Data:** Without a cursor column in your source data, Airbyte cannot track the last synced entry and cannot perform an incremental sync.
- **Database Type** : Enabling CDC (Change Data Capture) may require trade-offs like storage and performance. For example, PostgreSQL CDC requires creating a replication slot and a publication to capture WAL (Write-Ahead Log) within your database. This can significantly increase storage usage if not consumed frequently enough. So you might want to consider a full refresh of the underlying data instead.


#### DBT


Airbyte lands raw data; something else has to shape it. That’s DBT. It operates on a single database per model: it reads the raw data copied into the destination table, writes the transformed data back to the same destination database, and ideally provides a final schema that your application can consume.


It has become one of my favorite tools to work with due to its simplicity and capabilities. It’s lightweight and has proven reliable for our projects, since a model is just a SQL query with no framework to fight.


Note that DBT is a CLI tool, not a cluster like Airbyte, which matters because it has to run on a server (in this case, Airflow worker pods).


What follows are examples of how DBT models are structured and how easy it is to write tests to achieve a solid, production-ready data transformation layer.


For context, DBT models are .sql files, each holding a single query whose result becomes the final table. The filename will become the name of the final table. Here’s an example DBT query:


```text
select u.id as user_id,        u.first_name,        u.last_name,        p.country as country_of_origin  from user_entity u          join profile p on u.id = p.user_id  where p.domain = 'SOME_DOMAIN';
```


This model will generate a table with the columns: user_id, first_name, last_name, and country_of_origin. The data type for each column depends on the source data type unless you cast it in the SELECT statement.


In DBT, it’s possible to have dependencies between models. So if a table depends on another transformed table, you can reference the first model as shown in the following example:


```text
select u.id as user_id,        u.first_name,        u.last_name,        p.country as country_of_origin  from user_entity u          join {{ ref("profile") }} p on u.id = p.user_id  where p.domain = 'SOME_DOMAIN';
```


In this example, another model file named \`profile.sql\` is referenced. So DBT would know to build the table profile first, before building this model.


This is all you need for DBT to know that the second model depends on the first; it then handles the order of execution for you.


Additionally, in DBT you can add tests to your models. The simplest form of such a test involves writing another query; if it returns any results, the test is considered a failure. This gives you flexibility, as you can run your test cases within the database before deployment, which holds true for the transformation models as well.


Here’s an example of a test in DBT:


```text
select *  from {{ ref("user_info") }}  where user_id is null
```


This query should not return any values, as we expect user_id not to be null.


#### Airflow


Now that I’ve explained these first two components, I’ll move on to how they can interact. Airbyte and DBT have no integration, so we need a third tool to handle the most important tasks in any ELT solution: orchestrating between tools, providing visibility into each pipeline’s runs and scheduling runs. If you’ve worked on a centralized scheduler before, you know how complex it can get. That’s where Airflow comes in. It exposes per-task visibility and scheduling that a hand-rolled scheduler rarely matches.


What’s more, Airflow integrates with many tools, as its plugin ecosystem includes purpose-built providers for most sources. Additional packages must be installed for these integrations; however, they are specifically designed for Airflow and work seamlessly with the Airflow UI and Airflow servers.


Airflow has components that we use heavily in our system:


- **DAGs:** Runnable Python scripts that contain one or more tasks. Each DAG run usually performs a full data pipeline and ELT on your data. DAGs can be scheduled, or you can run them on demand.
- **Tasks:** Each task has a distinct use; tasks can be linked by having one task depend on another’s success.
- **Variables:** You can set variables or read them within your DAG Python script. This makes development easier. I’ll show some examples below.
- **Connections:** You can connect directly to a database system outside of Airbyte. This is useful if you need to query or write data in a centralized database for your DAG Python script business logic.


We don’t use Airflow only for data transformation. It’s an excellent scheduling tool for any need, including cron jobs and webhooks.


#### Integration between the three tools


Airflow is integrated with Airbyte and DBT as follows:


- **DBT:** Since it runs within Airflow worker pods, Airflow has full visibility into each component of DBT. So you can see each model being run for transformation and its tests’ success/failure, logs, etc.
- **Airbyte:** Airflow connects to Airbyte via Airbyte’s admin APIs. It uses a polling mechanism to check the status of a sync, but it’s more limited than what you see in a DBT task in Airflow. For example, you won’t have access to the Airbyte logs within the Airflow UI. But if an Airbyte task fails, you will see the API response Airbyte returns when polling the sync run’s status.


### Failure Modes: Pipeline Visibility Gaps and Concurrent Runs


Such visibility gaps are exactly where things quietly break. Airflow, as the core orchestrator, provides extensive metrics that you can use for alerting and monitoring your DAG runs and even tasks within each DAG. Here are some example alerts we use for our data pipelines:


- **DAG and task failures**
- **DAG runs skipped:** This is lower priority, but helpful to know if a DAG is taking significantly longer than expected, which can cause the next run to be skipped. With Airflow, you can investigate why a single DAG run is taking longer than expected.
- **DAGs removed:** Unfortunately, when you have a syntax error within your DAG Python script, Airflow won’t load the DAG at all. An unintentional change can cause the DAG to disappear after deployment without you noticing. This alert helps prevent that.


### Implementation: Orchestration-Driven Observability and Production-Readiness Practices


Knowing what breaks is one thing; designing so it doesn’t is another. To design a destination for your Airbyte, you’ll need a table that’s separate from the final table DBT produces. This is because Airbyte and DBT cannot integrate. We solve this by having these tables in different schemas. We create what we like to call a Landing Zone schema, as well as a final schema that the application consumes.


DBT recreates the transformed table (though you can configure it to be incremental) on each run. Initially, we granted the application’s user access to the tables DBT produced; however, we noticed that access was lost after each DBT run. So, make sure you update the default schema permissions for your application’s access at the schema level. You can automatically assign permissions to a database user with a query like the one below (this is for PostgreSQL, but a similar concept should be available for other databases):


```text
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA some_schema    GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO "some-user";
```


DBT performs transformations atomically, by swapping the table in a single transaction, so your application never reads a half-built table.


DBT profiles hold your database connections: target schema, credentials, and so on. They also define an important variable: the number of concurrent threads.


DBT is smart enough to figure out how many transformations it can run concurrently based on dependencies you define between your models.


#### Some other things to keep in mind


If you have two models where one depends sequentially on the other, you cannot go higher than one thread. But if you have four models, two of which depend on the other two, you can set the number of threads to two. This will transform two models at the same time and then process the next two that depend on the first two.


When using the Airbyte source for PostgreSQL, I noticed our data syncs can take more than 20 minutes when there is not much data to sync (especially in lower environments). After some research, I found a configuration called “Initial Waiting Time in Seconds (Advanced)”. This configuration defaults to 1200 seconds, so the Airbyte connection will wait that long for a change to appear before closing the sync. This can cause false-positive alerts for skipped DAG runs when your system doesn’t have many writes to the PostgreSQL database. To avoid this issue, reduce the setting, as a lower wait lets no-op syncs finish fast instead of tripping skipped-run alerts.


### Conclusion


Business requirements, team needs, and available technology tools can all change over time. Building your own self-hosted ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) solution gives you more control, more technical flexibility and more cost-effectiveness to deal with those changes than a SaaS solution. Airflow’s extensive integrations let you swap out any part of the ELT tools you’re using for another, without affecting the final result and with minimal changes to your data pipeline.


For example, we’re running into scalability issues with Airbyte, and this architecture lets us swap it out without a rewrite. Note that if you do choose this full ELT solution, you’ll need to get more involved in the nitty-gritty details of implementing it yourself. The trade-off is more control over your tools and their performance, but you lose the simplicity of a SaaS solution that provides a single-pane-of-glass ELT. I hope this article has clearly laid out how to weigh the two options. For us, the choice was clear.
